The goal is to uncover patterns that help explain why certain videos trend or perform better." format: html: code-tools: true code-overflow: wrap embed-resources: true editor: visual execute: warning: false echo: false jupyter: python3 --- # Abstract With millions of videos uploaded to YouTube daily, understanding what drives viewer engagement is essential for content creators. This project explores how key video attributes such as title wording, category, upload timing, and video duration influence engagement metrics like views, likes, and comments. Using a dataset of trending videos from India, the analysis focuses on uncovering patterns and predictors associated with higher performance. The goal is to generate actionable insights that support content strategy for new and growing channels. These findings will also help inform the early direction of a future educational YouTube channel and a creator-focused analytics concept currently in development. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Introduction Understanding what drives viewer interaction including views, likes, and comments has become crucial for content success. In this project, we explore how video metadata such as title length, upload timing, video duration, and like ratio correlate with viewer engagement. Our goal is twofold: - To uncover key patterns and features that influence a video’s performance. - To build predictive models that classify whether a video is likely to receive high engagement. Using a combination of exploratory data analysis and machine learning models like Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest, we identify which factors matter most. The findings can support creators, marketers, and data-driven platforms in optimizing video content strategies. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Research Questions 1. Which video attributes most influence engagement on YouTube? 2. Can we predict whether a video will achieve high engagement using metadata alone? 3. To generate meaningful insights on views by category, I’m mapping these IDs to their actual category names using available information from video titles and descriptions. ::: {#cell-Unique-categories .cell execution_count=4} ::: {#unique-categories .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ``` ::: ::: ::: {#predicting-category-description .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Unique category IDs: 15 Sample category IDs: [np.int64(1), np.int64(2), np.int64(10), np.int64(15), np.int64(17), np.int64(19), np.int64(20), np.int64(22), np.int64(23), np.int64(24), np.int64(25), np.int64(26), np.int64(27), np.int64(28), np.int64(29)] Unique inferred categories: 10 Inferred categories: ['Entertainment' 'Music' 'Other' 'People & Blogs' 'Gaming' 'Technology' 'News' 'Sports' 'Comedy' 'Howto & Style'] categoryId category_name 29 1 Other 136 2 Other 1 10 Music 51735 15 Other 19 17 Other 234 19 Other 5 20 Other 12 22 Other 10 23 Other 0 24 Other 15 25 News 30 26 Other 100 27 Other 70 28 Other 1698 29 Other ``` ::: ::: However, this approach often yields multiple category names for the same category ID, leading to inconsistencies. So I’m now taking a different approach by manually mapping category IDs based on patterns observed in sample videos. ::: {#cell-Analyzing-categories .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/analyzing-categories-output-1.png){#analyzing-categories width=944 height=560} ::: ::: ### Average Views by Category – Key Insight To make the analysis interpretable, we first mapped each categoryId to a meaningful label using a combination of: - Sample title and tag reviews from 1,000 randomly selected records - Heuristic keyword matching - Manual verification using known YouTube content types This mapping allowed us to group videos into intuitive categories like Music, Entertainment, Gaming, and Howto & Style. We then examined the average view count across these categories to understand what type of content resonates most with viewers in India. The analysis revealed that: - Pets & Animals and Music lead with the highest average views, showing strong emotional and entertainment appeal. - Movies, Science & Technology, and Sports also perform well, suggesting high engagement with trailers, tech demos, and events. - On the lower end, News & Politics and Nonprofits & Activism have lower average views, possibly due to niche audience interest or less viral potential. This insight helps identify which content types are more likely to trend useful for both content creators and recommendation systems aiming to boost visibility. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Exploratory Data Analysis ## Analyzing Missing Values: ::: {#missing-value-analysis .cell message='false' execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` missing_count missing_percent description 19455 7.74 video_id 0 0.00 publishedAt 0 0.00 title 0 0.00 channelTitle 1 0.00 categoryId 0 0.00 trending_date 0 0.00 channelId 0 0.00 tags 0 0.00 view_count 0 0.00 dislikes 0 0.00 likes 0 0.00 comment_count 0 0.00 thumbnail_link 0 0.00 comments_disabled 0 0.00 ratings_disabled 0 0.00 ``` ::: ::: Before creating new features, we examined the dataset for missing values: The dataset contains 251,277 rows and 16 columns - Most columns had no missing data - The only column with significant missingness was description (7.74% missing), a non-critical text field not used in modeling - One record had a missing channelTitle, which is negligible Conclusion: Since all relevant columns for feature engineering (e.g., title, publishedAt, view_count, likes) were complete, we proceeded without any imputation or row removal. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Impact of Upload Time (IST) on Average Views Analyzing the influence of upload time on the trending videos. ::: {#cell-AverageViews-by-UploadTime .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/averageviews-by-uploadtime-output-1.png){#averageviews-by-uploadtime width=1136 height=560} ::: ::: ### Average Views by Upload Hour - Key Insight After converting the publishedAt timestamps from UTC to Indian Standard Time (IST), we analyzed how the upload hour influences view counts. The trend reveals clear time-based engagement patterns: - Early morning uploads (1 AM to 3 AM IST) receive the highest average views, peaking at 2 AM, possibly because these videos are picked up by YouTube’s algorithm early and have full-day visibility. - Upload traffic drops significantly after 4 AM and remains low through the late morning and early afternoon (7 AM to 2 PM IST). - There's a modest recovery in the evening hours (6 PM to 10 PM), likely corresponding to post-work and post-school screen time, but not as strong as the early morning peak. - The lowest average views occur around 7 AM, suggesting it's the least favorable time to publish videos. This insight highlights the importance of timing for content release , especially for creators looking to maximize visibility and engagement in the Indian YouTube ecosystem. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Impact of Title Length on View Count Analyzing the impact of title length on the view count. ::: {#cell-title-length .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/title-length-output-1.png){#title-length width=1136 height=559} ::: ::: ### Average Views by Title Length - Key Insights To reduce noise from outliers, we grouped video titles into bins based on character count: - 0–30 - 31–60 - 61–90 - 91–120 The analysis shows that: - Titles with 61–90 characters had the highest average views - Very short (0–30) and moderately short (31–60) titles had lower performance - This suggests that moderate-to-long titles may be more effective at attracting clicks and generating views, possibly because they provide more context or keywords While title length alone isn’t a perfect predictor of success, this pattern highlights the importance of well-optimized, descriptive titles in YouTube content strategy. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Correlation Analysis ::: {#cell-Correlation-Matrix-NumericFeatures .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/correlation-matrix-numericfeatures-output-1.png){#correlation-matrix-numericfeatures width=885 height=560} ::: ::: ### Correlation Analysis - Key Insights We computed the Pearson correlation coefficients between all numeric features in the dataset. Key insights: - view_count has strong positive correlation with likes (0.80) and moderate correlation with comment_count (0.46).More likes and comments are naturally associated with higher views. - likes and comment_count also have a moderate correlation (0.62), suggesting videos that get liked also tend to receive more comments. - dislikes, title_length, upload_hour, and like_ratio show very weak or negligible correlation with view_count, indicating these may not be strong linear predictors. - trending_days has a small positive correlation with view_count (0.34), possibly because videos that trend longer accumulate more views though causality can go either way. Conclusion: While likes and comments are good indicators of engagement, some features like title length and upload hour may be more non-linear or contextual in their influence, which justifies using tree-based models that capture such interactions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Impact of Video Duration on View Count As video duration is one of the key metrics influencing the view count but it's not available in our primary data set, I am using the additional data fetched using the Youtube API to analyze this. ::: {#cell-Video-duration-Impact .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Saved file to /data/youtube_api_sample_with_duration.csv ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/video-duration-impact-output-2.png){#video-duration-impact width=943 height=559} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-Video-Duration-Category .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Average view count by duration category: duration_bin Short (<4 mins) 3.347441e+06 Long (10+ mins) 1.044555e+06 Medium (4-10 mins) 4.357051e+05 Name: viewCount, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/video-duration-category-output-2.png){#video-duration-category width=943 height=559} ::: ::: ### Short videos (\< 4 mins) had the highest average views Despite the wider spread, they outperform medium and long videos on average. Average Views: - Short (\<4 mins): \~2.45M - Medium (4–10 mins): \~1.33M - Long (10+ mins): \~0.85M The boxplot (log scale) clearly shows that: - Short videos have higher variability and more viral outliers - Long videos tend to perform more consistently, but generally get lower views While longer videos may offer more content, trending videos in our sample show a clear tilt toward shorter content. Videos under 4 minutes had the highest average views, possibly due to better retention and mobile-friendliness. This supports the rising popularity of short-form formats like YouTube Shorts and Reels. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Target Variable & Class Proportions We defined "High Performer" as the top 25% of videos by view count. This creates a classification problem where: - 25% of videos are labeled High Performer (target = 1) - 75% are labeled Low Performer (target = 0) This split was intentionally chosen to focus the model on identifying top-performing videos relative to the broader dataset. ::: {#cell-Defining-Target-Variable .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Class Counts: high_performer 0 188457 1 62820 Name: count, dtype: int64 Class Percentage: high_performer 0 74.999702 1 25.000298 Name: proportion, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/defining-target-variable-output-2.png){#defining-target-variable width=459 height=430} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Distribution of View Count Analyzing the distribution of view count, ::: {#cell-ViewCount-Distribution .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/viewcount-distribution-output-1.png){#viewcount-distribution width=945 height=461} ::: ::: ### Interpretation of View Count Distribution To better understand the natural distribution of video popularity, we plotted the histogram of view_count on a log scale. The results show a highly right-skewed distribution, a small number of videos gain a disproportionately large number of views, while the majority have relatively low view counts. This skew confirms the long-tail effect typical of platforms like YouTube, where a few viral videos dominate engagement. This justifies our choice to model the problem as a classification task by separating the top 25% (high performers) from the rest (low performers), rather than using raw view counts directly. ::: {#cell-ViewCount-Cumulative-Distribution .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} understand how views are distributed across videos, we analyzed the cumulative view share by video rank. - The plot shows the cumulative percentage of total views, as we move from the most-viewed to the least-viewed videos. - A clear skew is observed: the top 25% of videos (by count) contribute to over X% of total views. - This supports our choice of using the top 25% as the “High Performer” class for prediction, as these videos attract a disproportionately high share of user attention. - The long tail of less-viewed videos further emphasizes the class imbalance in the real-world popularity of videos. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Modeling & Evaluation ## Model Training ::: {#model-training .cell execution_count=16} ::: ![](index_files/figure-html/fitting-xgboost-model-output-3.png){#fitting-xgboost-model width=752 height=464} ::: ::: ### ROC Curve for XGBoost Model - Interpretation The ROC curve above illustrates the trade-off between the **true positive rate (sensitivity)** and **false positive rate** at various threshold settings for the XGBoost model. - The **orange curve** shows the model’s ability to distinguish between high and low performer videos. - The **Area Under the Curve (AUC)** is **0.84**, indicating strong discriminative performance. - AUC of 0.84 means there's an **84% chance** the model ranks a randomly chosen high performer video higher than a randomly chosen low performer. - The curve’s position well above the diagonal line (which represents random guessing) confirms that the model is significantly better than chance in predicting video engagement performance. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## ROC Comparison ::: {#cell-Comparing-Models-ROC .cell execution_count=19} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/comparing-models-roc-output-1.png){#comparing-models-roc width=944 height=560} ::: ::: ### ROC Curve Comparison – Model Performance - This chart compares the performance of four classification models based on their ROC curves and AUC scores: - **XGBoost** performs the best with an **AUC of 0.85**, indicating strong ability to distinguish between high and low engagement videos. - **Random Forest** closely follows with an **AUC of 0.84**, also showing robust predictive power. - **Logistic Regression** achieves an **AUC of 0.73**, offering a decent baseline but less nuanced decision boundaries. - **Decision Tree** lags with an **AUC of 0.70**, likely due to overfitting and limited generalization. Conclusion: Ensemble models (Random Forest and XGBoost) clearly outperform simpler models by capturing complex patterns in the data, making them more effective for this classification task. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Confusion Matrix ::: {#cell-Confusion-Matrix .cell execution_count=20} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/confusion-matrix-output-1.png){#confusion-matrix width=623 height=464} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` True Negatives: 44953 False Positives: 11580 False Negatives: 4914 True Positives: 13932 Precision: 0.55 Recall: 0.74 ``` ::: ::: ### Confusion Matrix - Key Insights - Precision (Top 25%): 13,966 / (13,966 + 11,448) ≈ 0.55 - Out of all videos predicted as Top 25%, 55% were actually Top 25%. - Recall (Top 25%): 13,966 / (13,966 + 4,880) ≈ 0.74 - The model correctly identified 74% of all actual Top 25% videos. - ROC AUC Score: \~0.85 - The model is quite good at ranking positives higher than negatives. The confusion matrix shows the model performs well in identifying high-performing videos (Top 25%). While there are some false positives, the recall of 74% indicates the model captures the majority of true top performers. With a ROC AUC of 0.85, this XGBoost model is a strong candidate for helping creators or platforms prioritize videos with high viral potential. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Feature Importance - XGBoost To better understand what drives model predictions, we analyzed **feature importance scores from the XGBoost model**. These scores reflect how much each feature contributed to improving the model’s performance during training. Higher importance indicates a stronger influence on the final prediction of whether a video is a high performer. This helps us not only interpret the model’s behavior but also identify which video attributes are most impactful for engagement. ::: {#cell-Important-Features .cell execution_count=21} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/important-features-output-1.png){#important-features width=944 height=559} ::: ::: This plot suggests: - Videos in the Music and People & Blogs categories, - Those with more trending days, and - Features like upload hour, like ratio, and title length all have strong influence on whether a video becomes a top 25% performer. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | |:-----------------------------------------------------------------------| | \# Answering Research Questions | | 1\. What video characteristics are associated with higher engagement? We explored several features from video metadata and found the following trends: | | \- Category: Some categories like Music and People & Blogs consistently dominated in view counts and were top predictors in our model. - Trending Days: Videos trending longer had significantly higher total views. - Publish Time: Uploads around evening hours (6–9 PM) showed relatively higher engagement. - Title Length: Titles of moderate length performed better, possibly due to clarity and catchiness. - Like Ratio: A strong predictor of performance, though not known in advance. - Video Duration (from YouTube API sample): - Short videos (\<4 mins) had the highest average view count, indicating strong virality potential. | | \#### Takeaway: Shorter videos in popular categories, posted at peak hours, are more likely to trend and engage users. | | 2\. Can we build a predictive model to identify high-performing videos? | | Yes, we framed this as a binary classification task to identify top 25% videos by view count. | | \- Best Model: XGBoost with tuned hyperparameters | | \- Performance: | | \- ROC AUC: 0.85 | | \- Precision: 0.55 | | \- Recall: 0.74 | | \- Key Predictors: | | \- Video category - Trending days - Upload hour - Title length - Like ratio | | 3\. Which model performs best in predicting high engagement? | | \- Both **Random Forest** and **XGBoost** performed well in predicting high-engagement videos, with **XGBoost slightly outperforming** the others in overall accuracy and AUC. | # Conclusion & Next Steps In this project, we explored how YouTube video metadata can be used to predict video engagement. After defining high-performing videos as those in the top 25% by views, we framed this as a binary classification problem and engineered features such as upload hour, title length, duration, and like ratio. Through exploratory analysis and modeling, we found: - **Upload timing** and **like ratio** were strong indicators of engagement. - **Ensemble models**, especially **XGBoost**, outperformed baseline models like Logistic Regression and Decision Tree in identifying high performers. - Our best model (XGBoost) achieved an **AUC of 0.85**, suggesting strong predictive capability using only metadata features ### Next Steps - **Enhance feature set** by incorporating additional metadata such as tags, sentiment of the title, or channel subscriber count and audience demographics. - **Personalize insights** by analyzing engagement patterns across different audiences or geographies. - **Deploy the model** as a tool to help content creators optimize their upload strategy and video design choices. - **Retrain periodically** using fresh data to adapt to evolving trends and platform algorithms. - This work lays the foundation for a scalable, data-driven assistant that can support YouTube creators in making more strategic content decisions.
